person.name: Hedy_Lamarr
person.summary: Hedy Lamarr (born Hedwig Eva Maria Kiesler) was an Austrian-born American film actress and inventor. Rising to fame in Europe with the controversial film Ecstasy (1933), she later became a Hollywood star in such films as Algiers (1938), Boom Town (1940), White Cargo (1942), and Samson and Delilah (1949). During the Second World War she co‑invented, with composer George Antheil, a frequency‑hopping "Secret Communication System" for torpedo guidance, an important precursor to modern spread-spectrum technologies used in wireless communication.

events.title: Birth in Vienna
events.description: Hedwig Eva Maria Kiesler, later known as Hedy Lamarr, was born to Jewish parents Gertrud "Trude" Kiesler (née Lichtwitz) and Emil Kiesler in Vienna, then part of Austria-Hungary. She grew up as an only child in a culturally sophisticated, upper-middle-class household.

images.caption: Flag of Austria, the country in which Hedy Lamarr was born in 1914.

events.date_note: Lamarr won a beauty contest in Vienna at age 12
events.title: Wins Vienna beauty contest
events.description: As a 12‑year‑old schoolgirl, Hedy Lamarr won a local beauty contest in Vienna. The experience, combined with her fascination with theater and film, encouraged her growing interest in performing and public appearance.

events.title: First film appearance
events.description: While working as a script girl at the Sascha-Film studios in Vienna, Hedy Lamarr made her first screen appearance as an extra in the romantic comedy film "Money on the Street" (Geld auf der Straße), marking the beginning of her professional film career.

events.title: Takes early leading roles
events.description: After small parts in Austrian films and a stage appearance in the play "The Weaker Sex" at the Theater in der Josefstadt, Hedy Lamarr moved to Berlin, where she received a role in Alexis Granowsky's film "The Trunks of Mr. O.F." and soon afterward her first leading role in the comedy "No Money Needed" (Kein Geld nötig). These roles established her as a promising young actress in German-language cinema.

events.date_note: Lamarr was cast in Ecstasy in early 1933 at age 18
events.title: Stars in Ecstasy
events.description: At age 18, Hedy Lamarr was cast in the lead role of Gustav Machatý's film "Ecstasy" (Ekstase). Her performance as a neglected young wife included scenes of nudity and simulated orgasm that made the film both celebrated and notorious, bringing her international attention and controversy.

events.title: Marries Friedrich Mandl
events.description: Hedy Lamarr married Austrian arms manufacturer Friedrich Mandl at the Karlskirche in Vienna. The marriage was highly controlling; Mandl attempted to curtail her acting career and kept her socially isolated, while exposing her to discussions of military technology at his business meetings.

events.date_note: In 1937 she traveled to London and met Louis B. Mayer there
events.title: Meets Louis B. Mayer
events.description: After arriving in London from Paris, Hedy Lamarr met Louis B. Mayer of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, who was scouting European talent. Initially rejecting his contract offer, she later sailed on the same liner to New York, where she negotiated a much higher salary and agreed to work for MGM under the name Hedy Lamarr.

events.date_note: Lamarr left Mandl and fled Austria in 1937; precise date uncertain
events.title: Escapes Mandl and Austria
events.description: Finding her marriage to Friedrich Mandl intolerable and disturbed by his connections to fascist regimes, Hedy Lamarr left both her husband and Austria. Accounts differ on the details, but she fled to Paris, ending the relationship and beginning her life as an independent actress in Western Europe.

events.title: Hollywood breakthrough in Algiers
events.description: Now promoted by MGM as "the world's most beautiful woman," Hedy Lamarr was loaned to producer Walter Wanger to star opposite Charles Boyer in the romantic drama "Algiers." Released in 1938, the film became a national sensation in the United States and established Lamarr as a major Hollywood star.

images.caption: Publicity still showing Sigrid Gurie, Charles Boyer, and Hedy Lamarr for the 1938 film "Algiers."

events.title: Stars in Boom Town
events.description: Hedy Lamarr co-starred with Clark Gable, Claudette Colbert, and Spencer Tracy in MGM's oilfield drama "Boom Town." The film was a major box-office success, reinforcing her status as a leading lady in high-profile Hollywood productions.

images.caption: Publicity photograph of Clark Gable and Hedy Lamarr for the 1940 MGM film "Comrade X," made the same year as "Boom Town."

events.date_note: U.S. patent 2,292,387 was filed 1940-06-10 and granted 1942-08-11; this event marks issuance
events.title: Patent for Secret Communication System
events.description: Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil were granted U.S. Patent 2,292,387 for their "Secret Communication System," a frequency-hopping radio guidance method designed to prevent jamming of Allied torpedoes during World War II. Although not implemented operationally at the time, their spread-spectrum concept later became foundational for secure wireless communication technologies.

images.caption: Page from the U.S. patent for Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil's "Secret Communication System."

events.title: Leads in White Cargo
events.description: Hedy Lamarr played the seductive character Tondelayo opposite Walter Pidgeon in MGM's drama "White Cargo." The film was a huge box-office hit, and her provocative line "I am Tondelayo. I make tiffin for you?" became one of her most remembered screen moments, exemplifying the exotic roles she was often given.

images.caption: Hedy Lamarr and Walter Pidgeon in a scene from the 1942 film "White Cargo."

events.title: Triumph with Samson and Delilah
events.description: Hedy Lamarr starred as Delilah opposite Victor Mature in Cecil B. DeMille's biblical epic "Samson and Delilah." Released in 1949, it became her most commercially successful film and one of the top box-office hits of the era, cementing her legacy as a major Hollywood star.

images.caption: Color publicity photograph of Victor Mature and Hedy Lamarr in costume for "Samson and Delilah" (1949).

events.title: Releases final feature film
events.description: Hedy Lamarr appeared in her final feature film in 1958, after which she largely withdrew from motion pictures, making only occasional television appearances. This marked the effective end of her three-decade screen career spanning European and Hollywood cinema.

events.title: Death in Florida
events.description: Hedy Lamarr died in Casselberry, Florida, at the age of 85. The Austrian-born actress and inventor left behind a complex legacy as both a Hollywood icon and a pioneer of spread-spectrum communication technology.

images.caption: Flag of California, representing the U.S. state where Lamarr spent much of her career before retiring to Florida.
